title: When the Storm Hits
author: Andrea Chiarelli
summary: Chiarelli argues that the real test of organisational culture is how people behave when something goes wrong, not what the onboarding slide says. A crisis magnifies existing behaviours, and under stress people fall back on fast, automatic habits, so the small unspoken rituals matter most. She makes the case through two short scenarios, one where a team protects itself and goes silent and one where a morning huddle habit lets a team admit errors and fix a system failure within hours. Edmondson, Schein and Kahn supply the research frame, with meaningfulness, safety and availability named as the conditions leaders can shape daily. The piece closes with reflective questions for leaders, including how their own reaction under pressure sets the tone.
points: Culture is revealed under pressure: espoused values on the wall matter less than rehearsed behaviour in the hardest hour.
Small, repeated rituals such as short daily huddles or asking what did we learn this week become automatic responses when a crisis hits.
Kahn's three conditions of meaningfulness, safety and availability determine whether people act, speak up or have the capacity to respond.
Leaders can use low-stakes moments as rehearsals and should examine how their own reaction under stress sets the team's tone.
quotes: A crisis - no matter how big or small - doesn’t create new behaviours, but simply magnifies existing ones.

This is the difference between the values that organisations support in an ideal world and project externally (described as “espoused values” by Shein) and what we actually do under stress. The gap between the two is where trust and morale collapse.

This response wasn’t improvised. The team had a habit of ten-minute huddles each morning, where everyone shared roadblocks openly. When the real storm hit, they didn’t freeze or blame. They just did what they’d practiced.
Amy Edmondson’s work on psychological safety shows that consistent, repeated behaviours - rituals of openness and candour - create environments where people feel safe to speak up.

If work feels meaningless, people won’t care enough to act. If psychological safety is absent, they’ll spot problems but stay silent. And if availability is drained by stress or overload, they simply won’t have the bandwidth to respond.

Leaders can’t control when a crisis arrives, but they can shape these conditions every day: through clarity of purpose, behaviours that make it safe to speak and realistic workloads that preserve capacity.

The next time you’re tempted to admire a glossy slide deck on culture, resist. Those words won’t tell you what really matters. As we have explored here, you will only see that in the crunch - when deadlines slip or when an upset client picks up the phone. In those moments, the rehearsed behaviours take over. If you want to learn what an organisation’s culture truly looks like, watch what happens in the hardest hour.
